nodes.name: Chemical exfoliation of MoS2
nodes.procedure: Chemical exfoliation of bulk MoS2 by the lithium intercalation method: intercalation process of lithium compounds (n-butyllithium) between MoS2 layers followed by furious exfoliation of Li-intercalated compounds via reacting with water.

unit_operations.name: Lithium Intercalation
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: intercalation process of lithium compounds (e.g., n-butyllithium) between MoS2 layers

unit_operations.name: Exfoliation
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: furious exfoliation of Li-intercalated compounds via reacting with water

nodes.source_text: Chemical exfoliation of bulk MoS2 by the lithium intercalation method is widely used to obtain single- or few-layered MoS2 nanomaterials. This method typically includes an intercalation process of lithium compounds (e.g., n-butyllithium) between MoS2 layers followed by a furious exfoliation of Li-intercalated compounds via reacting with water.

nodes.name: Ball-milling MoS2
nodes.procedure: Wu et al. synthesized MoS2 nanosheets with high active site density via a ball-milling-assisted microdomain reaction method by using MoO3 and S microparticles as the starting materials.

nodes.name: Solvothermal defect-rich MoS2
nodes.procedure: Xie et al. reported the large scale synthesis of the defect-rich MoS2 nanosheets with a thickness of ~5.9 nm in a solvothermal system. Excess thiourea in the reaction system played a crucial role in the formation of defect-rich nanosheet morphology.

unit_operations.name: Solvothermal Reaction
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: large scale synthesis of the defect-rich MoS2 nanosheets with a thickness of ~5.9 nm in a solvothermal system

nodes.source_text: Xie et al. reported the large scale synthesis of the defect-rich MoS2 nanosheets with a thickness of ∼5.9 nm in a solvothermal system (Fig. 9). The authors found that excess thiourea in the reaction system played a crucial role in the formation of defect-rich nanosheet morphology.

Electrodeposition of amorphous MoSx
nodes.procedure: Electrodeposition achieved by consecutive cyclic voltammetry measurements in an aqueous solution of (NH4)2[MoS4] at room temperature. By tuning the deposition parameters, the composition (MoSx, x=2-3) and thickness (40-150 nm) of MoSx can be controlled.

unit_operations.name: Cyclic Voltammetry Electrodeposition
unit_operations.procedure_snippet: consecutive cyclic voltammetry measurements in an aqueous solution of (NH4)2[MoS4] at room temperature

nodes.source_text: Electrodeposition is a simple and effective method to prepare MoSx. It can be simply achieved by consecutive cyclic voltammetry measurements in an aqueous solution of (NH4)2[MoS4] at room temperature.

nodes.name: Acidification synthesis of amorphous MoS3
nodes.procedure: Amorphous MoS3 obtained upon acidification of an aqueous mixture of MoO3 and Na2S.
nodes.source_text: Hu's group reported that amorphous MoS3 could be obtained upon acidification of an aqueous mixture of MoO3 and Na2S.

nodes.name: Hydrothermal WS2 nanosheets
nodes.procedure: Chhowalla's group synthesized WS2 nanosheets in a simple hydrothermal reaction system using tungsten chloride and thioacetamide as starting materials.
nodes.source_text: Chhowalla's group synthesized WS2 nanosheets in a simple hydrothermal reaction system for the first time. The selection of the starting materials (tungsten chloride and thioacetamide) was crucial for the formation of sheet-like WS2.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS confirmed presence of bridging S₂²⁻ or apical S²⁻ in MoS₂ nanosheet structure indicating unsaturated sulfur sites.
nodes.evidence_snippet: They confirmed the presence of bridging S₂²⁻ or apical S²⁻ in the nanosheet structure by XPS analyses, and the positive role of these unsaturated sulfur sites on HER performance of MoS₂ nanosheets.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS identified unsaturated S atoms as terminal S₂²⁻ and S²⁻ in amorphous MoSx.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The unsaturated S atoms were widely accepted to be catalytically active sites, and they were often identified as terminal S₂²⁻ and S²⁻ via XPS analysis.
